content_preview.title: Lava Finds 24,650 Internet-Exposed Server BMCs Leaking Password Hashes Through a 2013 IPMI Flaw
content_preview.summary: Security researchers found 24,650 of 36,872 internet-exposed server management interfaces leaking password hashes via a decades-old IPMI weakness, with one already targeted by a ransom note.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

More than 24,000 internet-exposed servers are leaking authentication password hashes from their Baseboard Management Controller (BMC) interfaces because of a weakness built into the IPMI 2.0 specification itself, according to [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-24-000-exposed-server-bmcs-leak-password-hash-via-decades-old-flaw/). Researchers at cybersecurity and infrastructure startup Lava scanned the public internet for IPMI services exposed on UD...

editor_notes.content_quality: Well-structured News piece (Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know), 550 words, within the 400-1200 word range for the News category. Neutral, non-sensational tone throughout; no AI self-reference. Every bullet in 'What We Know' carries an inline citation to one or both sources, and the 'What We Don't Know' section is an honest, accurate account of genuine gaps in the reporting rather than padding.
editor_notes.source_verification: MANDATORY source reading completed in full — no live WebFetch was used or needed; both snapshots saved successfully and were read from disk. (1) sources/2026-07/lava-finds-24650-internet-exposed-server-bmcs-leaking-password-hashes-through-a-2013-ipmi-flaw/source-0.html.gz (BleepingComputer, 'Over 24,000 exposed server BMCs leak password hash via decades-old flaw', by Bill Toulas, fetched via Archive.org fallback because the live BleepingComputer URL bot-blocked the fetch, per manifest.json archive_fallback:true / archive_url). Decompressed and re-hashed independently: sha256 b3721680da647b4f42fce6948191fa41cc151aecc2656be7d979ff30191a3bd6, which matches the manifest's recorded sha256 exactly, confirming the on-disk snapshot is intact and unmodified. Confirmed against this snapshot: the 24,000+/36,872/24,650 host counts, the 'at least a third... dictionaries and factory stickers' claim (verbatim match), the 6,240 empty-username and 2,340 weak-admin-password figures, the 39% US concentration on the live exposure map, the ~1-day-per-response HPE/Apple M3 cracking estimate, the 0.3 BTC ransom note on an exposed HPE iLO 4 page, Supermicro's stated plan to review its default password policy, and HPE's auto-response-only reply to Lava's outreach. All confirmed verbatim or near-verbatim. (2) sources/2026-07/lava-finds-24650-internet-exposed-server-bmcs-leaking-password-hashes-through-a-2013-ipmi-flaw/source-1.html.gz (The Hacker News, '24,650 Internet-Exposed BMCs Disclose IPMI Password Hashes Before Login', by Ravie Lakshmanan, fetched directly, status 200, no archive fallback). Independently re-hashed: sha256 c0c669e3e906e95050751c11df4911c1ed2ad1ab553d83991ee0f7f55f812592, matching the manifest exactly. Confirmed against this snapshot: CVE-2013-4786 / CVSS 7.5, the 36,872/24,650 counts, the Michael Katchinskiy quote ('More than 30% of the returned hashes were associated with passwords that could be recovered using common wordlists and predictable factory chassis-sticker formats') reproduced verbatim in the article, the Dell advisory quote fragment ('an inherent problem with the specification for IPMI v2.0') reproduced verbatim as a substring of Dell's full quoted sentence, the Supermicro ~1-hour recovery figure despite unique per-server passwords, and the recommended mitigations (block UDP 623, rotate passwords, disable legacy IPMI, restrict to private management networks). No hallucinated quotes or fabricated specifics were found in either source. Both cited URLs also appear in article.sources (no orphan-source / bidirectional gap). One editorial observation (not corrections-worthy, does not affect the verdict below): BleepingComputer estimates HPE factory-password recovery at ~1 day per response on an Apple M3, while The Hacker News separately states HPE iLO factory passwords were recoverable 'within a minute' using modern GPU hardware — a real discrepancy between the two sources on the same metric (likely different cracking hardware/methodology, CPU vs GPU). The article accurately attributes its 1-day figure to BleepingComputer specifically and does not misstate either source, but it does not surface or reconcile the conflicting Hacker News figure. Also note: the article attributes 'a weakness built into the IPMI 2.0 specification itself' to BleepingComputer, but that specific 'specification itself' framing appears in The Hacker News's language, not BleepingComputer's (BC frames it as 'a 20-year-old vulnerability... rooted in a protocol introduced in 2004'). The underlying fact is true and supported by both sources; only the specific outlet attribution for that phrasing is loose. Neither issue is a fabrication, headline/lead-breaking, or misattribution severe enough to affect the quality verdict, and neither is the reason for this REJECT (see below).
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: No fabricated or unsourced facts identified. Every number, date, quote, and named party in the body traces to one or both cited snapshots as documented above.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and professional; no sensationalism or editorializing.
editor_notes.originality: REJECTED on originality/duplicate-coverage grounds — see duplicate_coverage_investigation below. This is not a quality-based rejection; on the article's own merits it would have received APPROVE.
editor_notes.duplicate_coverage_investigation: This PR (#2063, 'Lava Finds 24,650 Internet-Exposed Server BMCs Leaking Password Hashes Through a 2013 IPMI Flaw') was flagged as one of three independent submissions covering the same underlying story: PR #2061 ('Over 24,650 Internet-Exposed Server BMCs Leak Password Hashes via 20-Year-Old IPMI Flaw', opened first, chronological priority) and PR #2062 ('Lava Researchers Find 24,650 Exposed Server BMCs Leaking IPMI Password Hashes via 20-Year-Old Flaw'), all three sourced from the same Lava research as reported by BleepingComputer and The Hacker News. Investigation procedure: (1) completed a full independent quality review of #2063 first (documented above) so a verdict was available regardless of the duplicate check's outcome; (2) checked PR #2061 status via `gh pr view 2061 --json state,mergedAt` — found OPEN at the time of the initial check, with no existing review file under src/content/reviews/2026-07/ matching 'bmc'/'ipmi'/'24650' (only this review's own file matched); (3) per instructions, actively polled #2061 (and #2062) synchronously with real, timed Bash checks (roughly every 45-60s) rather than ending the turn or backgrounding the wait indefinitely; (4) after approximately 2-3 minutes of polling, PR #2061 transitioned to MERGED (mergedAt 2026-07-28T16:20:44Z, merge commit d64ac2734ef7ec81f2570f78ab6f120ea0dd874d), with its own review (commit 7476300ee) verdict APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS. Outcome: per the duplicate-coverage rule, because PR #2061 merged and its article is now the surviving, published account of this story, PR #2063 is REJECTed as a duplicate regardless of its own (high) standalone quality. PR #2062 was not separately evaluated for merge/reject status since #2061's merge alone is dispositive.
editor_notes.security_note: The submission's two cited sources are BleepingComputer and The Hacker News, not lavahq.io directly (lavahq.io is the security startup whose research both outlets report on, but its site was not fetched or read as part of reviewing this submission). Both source snapshots were inspected in full and contained ordinary news-article HTML/text with no content resembling an AI-agent system prompt, hidden instructions, or any other prompt-injection pattern. No injected instructions were encountered or followed during this review.
concerns: Duplicate coverage: this story is now covered by the published/merged article from PR #2061; publishing this submission as well would be redundant.

Minor, non-dispositive: the article does not surface The Hacker News's conflicting 'within a minute' HPE password-recovery figure alongside BleepingComputer's '~1 day on an Apple M3' figure for the same metric.

Minor, non-dispositive: 'a weakness built into the IPMI 2.0 specification itself' is attributed to BleepingComputer but that exact framing is closer to The Hacker News's language; the underlying fact is accurate and supported by both sources.
recommendations: No rewrite recommended under v3.9.0 — REJECT is terminal and this submission is discarded. If Machine Herald wants to revisit the two minor sourcing nuances noted above for future coverage of this research area, a fresh submission on a new angle (e.g. follow-up on organizational responses) could address them.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: On independent merits this submission would have received APPROVE: sources verified, quotes verbatim, numbers accurate, tone neutral, no fabrications. However, PR #2061 covering the identical story was merged during this review, making this submission a duplicate of now-published coverage. Verdict: REJECT, duplicate coverage of PR #2061.
